7.1.l: Pediatric Hip — Septic Arthritis & Transient Synovitis of the Hip
7.1.b:
Two diseases share one picture, an irritable hip, and missing the wrong one costs a femoral head.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is a septic hip?"
- "A pyogenic infection of the hip joint: a **surgical emergency**."
- "Half the children are **under 2 years**; the neonate shows almost no signs."
- "Treatment is **drainage, reduction and antibiotics**, never antibiotics alone."

### Septic Arthritis
The hip is the joint where infection does the most lasting harm.
- **Septic arthritis**: bacteria in the joint, usually from the blood
[[FIG: Fig 7.1 · 7.1
- It is a **surgical emergency**: the pus destroys cartilage and kills the head (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- The hip is the commonest septic joint in children and neonates

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| Peak age | first few years of life |
| Under 2 years | ≈**50%** of cases |
| Hip share | ≈**35%** of all septic joints |
| Knee share | ≈35% |
| Lower-limb joints | 61–79% (Campbell) |

- Severe sequelae come mainly in **children**, after a delayed diagnosis
- About **25–50%** of septic joints lose function permanently

### Transient Synovitis
The commonest cause of a painful hip in a child is harmless.
- **Transient synovitis**: a short-lived, non-infective inflammation of the hip synovium
- Other names: toxic synovitis, irritable hip
- It is the commonest cause of hip pain under **10 years**
- Full details → 7.10

MEMORY HOOK — the twins
- Septic arthritis and transient synovitis are twins in the same pram: they look alike, but one bites. Prove which twin you have before you go home.

7.2.l: Pediatric Hip — Septic Arthritis & Transient Synovitis of the Hip
7.2.b:
The child's hip anatomy lets bone and joint infect each other; hip anatomy itself → 01 Approach.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why is the child's hip special?"
- "The proximal femoral **metaphysis is intracapsular**, so osteomyelitis bursts into the joint."
- "Under **18 months**, transphyseal vessels carry infection into the epiphysis."
- "A tense effusion squeezes the retinacular vessels → **AVN**."

### Routes of Infection
Three roads lead bacteria into a joint.
- **Haematogenous** seeding: the commonest
- Spread from adjacent **osteomyelitis** of the metaphysis
- Direct inoculation: injection, trauma or surgery

### Intracapsular Metaphysis
Four joints let the metaphysis drain straight into the joint.
- Proximal femur, proximal humerus, proximal radius, distal tibia and fibula (Miller)
[[FIG: Fig 7.2 · 7.2
- Here metaphyseal pus decompresses into the joint
- So a septic hip often hides an **osteomyelitis**, and the reverse
- "Joint infection only, no bone" is not an acceptable answer in these joints

| Joint | Intracapsular part |
|---|---|
| **Hip** | proximal femoral metaphysis |
| Shoulder | proximal humeral metaphysis |
| Elbow | radial neck |
| Ankle | lateral malleolus (distal fibula) |

### Transphyseal Vessels
Age decides whether the physis is a barrier.
- In infants under **18 months**, vessels cross the physis (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 7.3 · 7.2
- They link metaphysis and epiphysis in hip, shoulder, elbow and ankle, not the knee
- So infection spreads from metaphysis to epiphysis and joint
[[FIG: Fig 7.4 · 7.2
- In a child, the avascular physis blocks spread; after closure, the vessels reunite
- Infection can even **separate the epiphysis** in a young child
[[FIG: Fig 7.5 · 7.2

### Mechanism of Destruction
Time is cartilage.
- Enzymes from bacteria and leucocytes may damage cartilage within **8 hours** (Orthobullets)
- Ground substance depletion begins at ≈**2 days**
- Cartilage destruction is apparent at **4–6 days**
- In infants, each day before surgery worsens the result
[[FIG: Fig 7.6 · 7.2
- Delay of ≈2.5 days: 25% poor results; ≈4.7 days: 50% (Lee 2015)
- A tense effusion raises intracapsular pressure → **osteonecrosis** of the head
- The distended capsule lets the head sublux, then **dislocate**

- Candidates name only the intracapsular metaphysis
- Say → "**infant transphyseal vessels, intracapsular metaphysis, structures crossing from metaphysis into the joint, and septicaemia**"

7.3.l: Pediatric Hip — Septic Arthritis & Transient Synovitis of the Hip
7.3.b:
Age picks the organism, and the organism picks the antibiotic.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which organism, at which age?"
- "***Staphylococcus aureus*** at every age."
- "Neonate: add **group B streptococcus** and gram-negative bacilli."
- "Toddler: think ***Kingella kingae***; sickle cell: think ***Salmonella***."

| Age (Campbell) | Usual organisms |
|---|---|
| **Under 3 months** | *S. aureus*, *E. coli* and other gram-negatives, group B streptococcus, *Candida* |
| **3 months – 5 years** | *S. aureus*, ***Kingella kingae***, group A streptococcus, pneumococcus, *H. influenzae* b (unimmunized) |
| **Over 5 years** | *S. aureus*, group A streptococcus |
| Sexually active adolescent | add *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* |

### Neonates
The neonatal unit brings its own bugs.
- *S. aureus*, including MRSA (methicillin-resistant *S. aureus*), leads in hospitalized neonates
- Intravenous catheters and hyperalimentation carry it in
- Risk factors: prematurity, caesarean section, NICU (neonatal intensive care unit) stay
- Umbilical or venous catheters and **heel puncture** cause transient bacteraemia

### Kingella kingae
A quiet organism of the toddler.
- Commonest at **6–36 months** (Campbell)
- Milder infection; fever may be absent
- It grows poorly on solid media: blood-culture bottles or **PCR** (polymerase chain reaction) find it
- Susceptible to most penicillins and cephalosporins

### Other Organisms
Special hosts have special organisms.
- **Sickle cell disease**: *Salmonella*, *S. aureus*, pneumococcus (Miller)
- *H. influenzae* b is now rare where children are vaccinated
- Community-acquired MRSA needs more operations and stays bacteraemic longer

MEMORY HOOK — the king of toddlers
- *Kingella* is the king of toddlers: it rules from 6 to 36 months, speaks softly (low fever) and hides from the culture plate.

7.4.l: Pediatric Hip — Septic Arthritis & Transient Synovitis of the Hip
7.4.b:
A child with a septic hip looks ill; a neonate with a septic hip may look almost well.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does a septic hip present?"
- "Child: fever, toxic look, **refuses to bear weight**, hip held flexed, abducted, externally rotated."
- "Neonate: **pseudoparalysis**, no fever, normal white count; only ESR and CRP rise."
- "A neonatal 'dislocated hip' is septic until proven otherwise."

### The Child
The picture is acute and loud.
- Acute pain, **limp** or refusal to bear weight
- Fever and a **toxic** appearance
- Severe pain on any passive movement

#### Posture
- The hip rests in **flexion, abduction and external rotation**
[[FIG: Fig 7.7 · 7.4
- In this position the capsule holds the most fluid, so pain is least
- A Thomas test shows a fixed flexion deformity

#### Movement
- The child will not move the hip: **pseudoparalysis**
- Every range is painful, internal rotation most
- Examine the spine and adjacent joints: infection may sit next door

### The Neonate
Here the inflammatory response is blunted.
- Neonate = the first **28 days**; the lecture used two months
- **No fever**: the immune system is immature (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- White cell count **normal**; ESR and CRP still rise
- Clues: irritability, poor feeding, crying when the nappy is changed
- One leg moves; the septic leg lies still: **pseudoparalysis**
- Infection at another site, such as an umbilical catheter, may be the only finding

#### Risk History
- Incubator stay, previous blood sampling, **septicaemia**
- Risk history plus a still limb = septic hip until proven otherwise
- In a neonate with one septic joint, scan **both hips**: signs are muted

#### Pathological Dislocation
- Pus distends the capsule, so the head subluxes, then dislocates
[[FIG: Fig 7.8 · 7.4
- A neonatal dislocation on ultrasound or arthrogram is septic until proven otherwise
- Do not label it DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip)

PITFALL — waiting for fever
- The neonate stays afebrile with a normal white count
- Say → "**in a neonate I do not wait for fever: a still leg plus raised ESR and CRP means ultrasound and aspiration now**"

MEMORY HOOK — the quiet baby
- A septic neonate is a quiet alarm: no fever, no white cells, only a leg that will not dance while the other kicks.

7.5.l: Pediatric Hip — Septic Arthritis & Transient Synovitis of the Hip
7.5.b:
Clinical prediction rules turn four or five simple findings into a probability.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what are the Kocher criteria?"
- "Fever **>38.5 °C**, non-weight bearing, ESR **>40 mm/h**, WBC **>12,000/mm³**."
- "Four of four: ≈**99%** septic; none: under **0.2%**."
- "Add **CRP >20 mg/L** (Caird); CRP plus non-weight bearing alone gives 74%."

### Kocher Criteria
Four predictors separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis.

| Predictor (Kocher) | Positive when |
|---|---|
| Fever | **>38.5 °C** (101.3 °F) |
| Weight bearing | **unable** |
| ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) | **>40 mm/h** |
| WBC (white blood cell count) | **>12,000/mm³** |

| Predictors present | Probability of septic arthritis (Orthobullets) |
|---|---|
| **4** | ≈**99.6%** |
| **3** | ≈**93%** |
| 0 | <0.2% |

- More than 90% of children with 3 of 4 criteria are septic
- The lecturer quotes **99%** with all four

### C-Reactive Protein and Caird
CRP is now the single most useful test.
- Caird added **CRP >20 mg/L** (2.0 mg/dL) as an independent predictor
- Order of strength: fever > CRP > ESR > non-weight bearing > WBC (Orthobullets)
- A high CRP counts even when the ESR is not yet high

#### Two-Variable Rule
| CRP >20 mg/L | Cannot bear weight | Probability (Campbell) |
|---|---|---|
| yes | yes | **74%** |
| yes | no | 15% |
| no | yes | 6% |
| no | no | **<1%** |

#### Behaviour of the Markers
| Marker | Rises | Peaks | Normal again |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CRP** | within **6 hours** | 2 days | ≈1 week of good treatment |
| **ESR** | slowly | 3–5 days | ≈3 weeks |

- So **CRP** follows treatment; ESR lags
- ESR is unreliable in neonates, sickle cell disease and in the first 48 hours

### Synovial Fluid
The aspirate gives the answer the blood only suggests.

| Fluid | Leucocytes/mm³ | Neutrophils (Campbell) |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | <200 | <25% |
| Toxic (transient) synovitis | 5,000–15,000 | <25% |
| **Septic arthritis** | **>80,000** | **>75%** |

- Miller and Orthobullets treat **>50,000** cells as septic
- Send Gram stain, culture and sensitivity, cell count; take blood cultures

MEMORY HOOK — the hot, limping, angry blood
- Kocher's four: the child is hot (fever), lame (no weight), and the blood is angry twice (ESR and WBC). Caird adds the fire alarm: CRP.

7.6.l: Pediatric Hip — Septic Arthritis & Transient Synovitis of the Hip
7.6.b:
Imaging finds the fluid; only the needle tells whether it is pus.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you image a suspected septic hip?"
- "**Ultrasound** first: an effusion, and a guide for the needle."
- "X-ray: often normal early; widened joint space, lateral displacement, subluxation."
- "**MRI** when osteomyelitis or abscess is suspected, if it does not delay drainage."

### Plain Radiographs
The film is normal early, so a normal film proves nothing.
- AP (anteroposterior) pelvis, and frog-lateral if the hip allows
- **Widened** medial joint space and soft-tissue swelling
- Infant: the femur displaced **laterally** by a tense effusion: much pus
- Later: subluxation, dislocation, metaphyseal osteomyelitis
[[FIG: Fig 7.9 · 7.6

### Ultrasound
The quickest, cheapest and radiation-free test.
- Shows even small **effusions** and capsular distension
[[FIG: Fig 7.10 · 7.6
- In the neonate it shows **pus around the head** and **instability**
[[FIG: Fig 7.11 · 7.6
- It **cannot** tell pus from serous fluid (Handbook)
- It guides **aspiration**
- No effusion makes septic arthritis unlikely

### Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI shows what is around the joint.
- Joint effusion and **adjacent osteomyelitis** or abscess
[[FIG: Fig 7.12 · 7.6
- Contrast shows a poorly perfused epiphysis at risk of AVN
[[FIG: Fig 7.13 · 7.6
- It separates septic hip from **pyomyositis** and psoas abscess
[[FIG: Fig 7.14 · 7.6
- It may be hard to get quickly, and a child may need sedation
- Never let MRI delay drainage of a hip full of pus

### Bone Scan and Computed Tomography
Second-line tests.
- Bone scan is sensitive but not specific; Campbell does not rely on it
- CT shows abscesses and guides aspiration, at a radiation cost

PITFALL — the dry ultrasound in the neonate
- Thick pus may look echogenic and small
- Say → "**a high-risk neonate with a still leg and raised CRP is aspirated even if the ultrasound is equivocal**"

Aspiration is the definitive test, and in the hip it is also part of treatment.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you aspirate a child's hip?"
- "Fully aseptic, in theatre or under ultrasound, before antibiotics."
- "Anterior: **2.5 cm lateral and 2.5 cm distal** to the femoral artery at the inguinal ligament."
- "A dry tap does **not** exclude pus: confirm the needle with an arthrogram."

### Indications
Aspirate when the criteria point to infection.
- Kocher or CRP criteria present, plus an **effusion** on ultrasound
- Criteria present and no ultrasound available
- Any doubt or mixed findings
- Aspirate **before** the first antibiotic dose whenever possible

### Technique
Three routes reach the joint; image intensification makes the needle certain.
[[FIG: Fig 7.15 · 7.7

| Route (Campbell) | Entry | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| **Anterior** | 2.5 cm lateral, 2.5 cm distal to the femoral artery at the inguinal ligament | 45°, medially and proximally, 5–7.5 cm |
| **Lateral** | just anterior and inferior to the greater trochanter | 45°, along the neck, 5–10 cm |
| **Medial** | below the adductor longus tendon, hip flexed and abducted | below the femoral artery to the head |

- Medial route: the needle passes under the adductor longus
[[FIG: Fig 7.16 · 7.7
- Use full **aseptic** conditions: a careless needle introduces infection
- Ultrasound guidance shows the needle in the effusion
- If nothing comes out, inject contrast: an **arthrogram** proves the needle position

### The Negative Tap
The hip hides pus better than the knee.
- In the knee the needle is surely in the joint; in the hip, never quite
- **Thick pus** may not come through the needle
- So a dry tap does not exclude pus (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- If signs persist, explore the hip

### Repeated Aspiration
The lecturer uses a second tap to decide.

| Next-day aspiration | Action (Prof Abdel-Ghani) |
|---|---|
| No re-collection, or a little | continue antibiotics |
| Same amount | aspiration will not work → **open** |
| More than before | **open** |
| CRP still rising | **open** |

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you treat a septic hip?"
- "**Urgent arthrotomy** and washout, through an **anterior** approach in a small child."
- "Keep the head **reduced**: Pavlik or spica in abduction; it obliterates the dead space."
- "Antibiotics by age, IV then oral, ≈**3–4 weeks**, until CRP normalises."

### Principles
Do not wait once pus is found.
[[FIG: Fig 7.17 · 7.8
- Pus found → **drain** now
- Treat the infection and the hip **together**
- **Never antibiotics alone** for a septic hip with pseudoparalysis
- In doubt, open and drain: an unneeded arthrotomy rarely harms

#### Dead Space
- Any infection needs its **dead space** obliterated
- A head outside the socket leaves the acetabulum empty: pus collects there
- Then no antibiotic controls the infection
- A reduced head closes the space; the CRP then falls (Prof Abdel-Ghani)

| | Head reduced | Head outside |
|---|---|---|
| Dead space | obliterated | empty acetabulum |
| Antibiotic response | good | poor |
| Head remnant | may survive and grow | erodes and disappears |
| Acetabulum | grows around the head | stays shallow |

PITFALL — "resistant to antibiotics"
- A child on antibiotics for days with a CRP that will not fall is labelled resistant
- Say → "**it is not resistance: the hip has not been drained and reduced**"

### Antibiotics Alone
Very few septic hips escape surgery.
- Antibiotics alone are rarely indicated
- Exception: adolescent **gonococcal** arthritis, which responds to penicillin
- Aspiration plus antibiotics may suffice if ESR and CRP fall quickly

### Arthrotomy
Open drainage is the standard for the hip.

#### Choice of Approach
| Approach | Use | Note (Campbell) |
|---|---|---|
| **Anterior** (Smith-Petersen interval) | small children: preferred | spares the head's blood supply, lowest dislocation risk, clear landmarks |
| **Medial** (Ludloff) | infant; pus tracking medially | behind adductor longus and pectineus |
| Lateral | anterior capsule through vastus lateralis | rarely used |
| **Posterior** (Ober) | adults: dependent drainage | risks the MFCA (medial femoral circumflex artery) and dislocation |

- The posterior approach must spare **quadratus femoris**: it carries the head's vessels
- Never use the posterior approach in a small child

#### Anterior Technique
- Vertical incision from **1 cm below the ASIS** (anterior superior iliac spine)
[[FIG: Fig 7.18 · 7.8
- Interval: **sartorius** medially, tensor fasciae latae laterally
- Retract **rectus femoris** medially to reach the capsule
- Protect the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve proximally
- Open the capsule; a 1 × 1 cm **capsular window** limits re-collection
- Send pus and synovium for culture; also the aspirate from the day before
- Wash with plenty of **saline**; leave the capsule open
- Close the skin loosely over a drain

#### Medial Technique
- 7.5–10 cm incision over the proximal adductor longus and gracilis
- Pass posterior to adductor longus and pectineus
- The abscess communicates with the joint behind the iliopsoas

### Neonatal Details
The lecturer's neonatal routine guards a 2–3 kg baby.
- Approach beside the **sartorius**, straight onto the capsule (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Remove pus, **not bone**: leave any head remnant, even one that looks dead
- Do not curette the tiny neck; it may already be broken by osteomyelitis
- **No antibiotic wash**: gentamicin is absorbed by the neonate
- Wipe off the povidone-iodine skin prep quickly for the same reason
- Drain: a soft **Nelaton** catheter, not a bulky corrugated drain that blocks reduction
- The neonatal wound closes in 48 hours; the drain keeps it open 2–3 days

### Reduction and Splintage
Reduction is part of the operation, not a later step.
[[FIG: Fig 7.19 · 7.8

| Device | Use |
|---|---|
| **Pavlik harness** | neonate: applied in theatre (Prof Abdel-Ghani) |
| Double **spica** in moderate abduction | infant: windowed for the wound |

- Keep the Pavlik until the hip is **clinically stable** and the CRP normal
- A late dislocation with a damaged head: skeletal traction first, then gentle reduction

A newer, less invasive drainage.
- Arthroscopic washout of the septic hip shows promising results in small studies
[[FIG: Fig 7.20 · 7.8
- High-volume lavage, at least **30 L** of saline, with no antibacterial additives
- No capsulotomy, to avoid leakage; two suction drains

- IV is not a must; it is forced only when no oral drug fits the culture

- Short courses also work: IV for 2–4 days, then oral, 2 weeks in uncomplicated cases (Pääkkönen 2017)

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is transient synovitis?"
- "A self-limiting synovitis: boys **4–8 years**, often after a cold."
- "Low or no fever, normal or mildly raised markers, **better within 1–2 days**."
- "Rest and NSAIDs; resolves in **1–2 weeks**; it does **not** cause Perthes."

### Epidemiology and Aetiology
The child is the same child who gets Perthes disease.
- About **3%** of children aged 3–10 years
- Peak **4–8 years**; boys twice as often (Handbook)
- Cause unknown: viral upper respiratory infection, post-streptococcal, minor trauma, allergy
- Some give an antihistamine in a resistant case

### Clinical Features
The story, not the examination, makes the diagnosis.
- Sudden hip, groin or thigh pain; limp or refusal to bear weight
- Fever **absent** or low-grade; the child does not look toxic
- Hip held in semi-flexion, abduction and external rotation, the low-pressure position
- **Internal rotation** is lost most: it raises intracapsular pressure

#### Diurnal Pattern
- Worst in the **morning**: a night of immobility increases congestion (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Movement through the day eases it: the child walks by evening
- A limp improving by evening, without fever, is reassuring

#### The Fever Question
- Ask: was there fever, and did it rise or fall after the limp began?
- A cold 3–4 days before is the typical story
- Rising fever after the limp began points to septic arthritis

### Investigations
Each test aims to exclude a worse disease.
- Labs: ESR usually **<20 mm/h**; CRP **<20 mg/L** best rules out sepsis
- **Ultrasound**: effusion and capsular distension, often in both hips
[[FIG: Fig 7.32 · 7.10
- X-ray: usually normal; take it if pain persists beyond **2 days** (Handbook)
- Aspiration: serous fluid = transient synovitis; pus = septic arthritis
- A POCUS (point-of-care ultrasound) rule: age 3–10, fever <38 °C, bearing weight, effusion → transient synovitis
[[FIG: Fig 7.33 · 7.10
- **MRI** if no response after **2 weeks**: early Perthes, AVN or another cause

### Masking by Antibiotics
Antibiotics blur the picture.
- A viral illness treated with antibiotics may hide septic arthritis
- The picture improves, then the doubt remains
- An unneeded arthrotomy is the lesser error; a missed septic hip destroys the joint

### Treatment
Rest the joint and wait.
- **Rest**: no jumping, no sport, no physical education
- **NSAIDs** (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs); symptoms ease within 24–48 hours
- Partial weight bearing; bed rest if severe; traction rarely helps
- Complete resolution in ≈**2 weeks**
- **Recurrence** in up to **20%** (Orthobullets): warn the parents

### Warning Features
These children are not simple transient synovitis.

| Feature | Think of | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Fever, toxic look, Kocher criteria | septic arthritis | aspiration |
| No improvement in **3 days** (Handbook) | septic arthritis, osteomyelitis | re-examine, markers, aspirate |
| Recurrent episodes | Perthes disease | X-ray, MRI |
| Not better after **2 weeks** | early Perthes, AVN | MRI |
| Bilateral, persistent | rheumatological disease | rheumatology work-up |

### Relation to Perthes Disease
An old link has been broken.
- Transient synovitis was once thought to lead to Perthes disease
- There is **no** real relation (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Perthes found later was Perthes from the start, with its synovitis mistaken for transient synovitis
- Literature figures of 0–10% are disputed → 05 Perthes Pathology

- Long-acting penicillin prophylaxis is the cardiologist's decision, not the orthopaedist's
